title: Content Security Policy in Practice

source_subtopics.title: Deploying CSP without breaking application functionality

subtopics: Deploying CSP without breaking application functionality
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Content Security Policy in Practice.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for Content Security Policy in Practice and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for Content Security Policy in Practice, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 10: Cross-Site Scripting and Client-Side Security. It builds practical understanding of Content Security Policy in Practice with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Content Security Policy in Practice addresses how untrusted data or requests cross a boundary and may influence application behavior. The safe fix should address the root cause and remain testable. Use standards-based browser/transport controls that fit the deployment, test their effects in a staging environment, and never assume a header replaces correct server-side access checks.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Content Security Policy in Practice can be understood through this sequence: Inspect request/response → Identify boundary mismatch → Apply narrow control → Test deployment behavior. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 73.1 CSP sources and directives; 73.2 Nonces and hashes; 73.3 Report-only policies; 73.4 Third-party resource restrictions; 73.5 Deploying CSP without breaking application functionality; 73.6 CSP limitations and complementary defenses. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Use standards-based browser/transport controls that fit the deployment, test their effects in a staging environment, and never assume a header replaces correct server-side access checks.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: Content Security Policy in Practice
content_blocks.code:
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
content_blocks.expected_output: A response declares a restrictive baseline for resource loading, framing, MIME sniffing, and referrer disclosure.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Review the directives against the application’s needed resources and embedding use cases; test in staging and avoid deploying a copied policy without compatibility review.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Use standards-based browser/transport controls that fit the deployment, test their effects in a staging environment, and never assume a header replaces correct server-side access checks. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Content Security Policy in Practice”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Content Security Policy in Practice in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Content Security Policy in Practice is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Use standards-based browser/transport controls that fit the deployment, test their effects in a staging environment, and never assume a header replaces correct server-side access checks.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
